schools.summary: Gill pictures the pause — Elihu waited to see if any would contradict or if Job would reply, then resumed to refute other undue expressions Job had let fall.
Clarke gives the argument of the speech in precis: Elihu charges Job with impious speeches, denies man can affect or profit God, and holds that few of the afflicted cry to God in faith.

Henry marks Elihu's method — appealing to Job's own conscience ('Thinkest thou this to be right?') and recurring to his maxim that God is greater than man — with a good opinion of Job, whom he would recall from a rash word.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'my righteousness exceedeth God's' (the preposition comparative, cf. ch. 32:2), taking the charge as it stands; Ellicott holds Job never said it in so many words, though his words were capable of being so represented — a misrepresentation.

Clarke calls it a blasphemous saying Job never uttered, rendering rather 'I am righteous before God' — a character God himself gave him; Wesley: Job said only things from which it might seem to follow, that God punished him beyond desert.
Gill takes the appeal to Job's own conscience: on reflection he could never think right what he had said of God and his justice, letting the charge stand as a fair inference.

debates.question: Did Job really say 'My righteousness is more than God's,' and does the Hebrew warrant it?

sides.position: A misrepresentation; Job never said it, and the clause is better rendered 'I am righteous before God'
The charge stands, the preposition comparative — 'my righteousness exceedeth God's'

themes: My righteousness is more than God's

schools.summary: Gill grants Job seemed to say his righteousness was of no avail, yet insists it is inferred, not asserted, and distinguishes: one's own righteousness profits not for justification but for much else (defence, honour, a good conscience).

Clarke: 'My righteousness cannot profit thee, nor benefit myself'; Wesley reads 'unto thee' as 'unto me' (a change of person) — 'God does not reward me as I deserve' — but it was unfair to charge this on Job, who never affirmed it.

themes: What profit if I be cleansed from my sin

schools.summary: Gill: 'thy companions' are not the three friends (who side with Elihu) but all of Job's mind anywhere; the one answer confutes them all.
Clarke: 'I will show thee the evil of a sinful way and the benefit of righteousness, and supply what thy friends omitted.'
Ellicott notes Elihu only repeats Eliphaz (ch. 22:3) and Bildad (ch. 25): God is too high to be affected by man, yet it does not follow he is indifferent, else no righteous judge.

outliers.note: Warns that Elihu's premise — God too exalted to be touched by human conduct — is true but, pushed too far, would make God indifferent and so unsay the very justice Elihu rose to defend.

themes: I will answer thee and thy companions
God too high to be affected

schools.summary: Henry turns the upward glance into the premise: heavens and clouds far above us, God infinitely above them, so out of reach of our sins or services; look up and worship the Lord of that host (Ps. 8:1; ch. 11:8).
Clarke glosses 'clouds' as shechakim / 'ethers,' from a root 'to contend' — agitated conflicting air and light; Wesley: they are above us, God above them, out of reach of our sins or services.
Gill keeps it physical: the firmament with sun, moon, and stars, and the clouds set above.

themes: God out of reach of our sins or services

schools.summary: Gill: sin is truly against God — against his nature, law, authority — yet cannot ruffle his peace or dethrone him; men can no more reach him than pluck the sun from its orbit; nor make any atonement ('what canst thou work for him?').

Henry: the malice of sinners is impotent malice — it cannot destroy God's being, dethrone him, disturb his peace, defeat his counsels, or derogate from his glory; so Job spoke amiss asking what he gained by being cleansed.
Clarke: God is neither benefited by righteousness nor injured by iniquity, however multiplied.
Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet in its logic, the heaping of transgressions only sharpening that their sum touches nothing above the clouds.

themes: no atonement in a sinner's hand

schools.summary: Gill roots all righteousness in God — angels', Adam's, Christ's imputed, grace implanted, works by his strength — so a man gives God nothing of his own; works add to his manifestative but not his essential glory (Ps. 16:2).

Henry by God's self-sufficiency: he needs not our service; our religion brings no accession to his felicity; we are beholden to him for making and accepting our righteousness, so can demand nothing but should be thankful.
Gill: wickedness wounds oneself (body, estate, soul) and one's neighbours; God resents and punishes it though, strictly, it cannot hurt him.
Clarke renders 'to a man like thyself is thy wickedness, and to the son of man thy righteousness' — the moral weight discharged sideways on one's fellows, never upward.
Henry: men are bettered or damaged by us, our goodness extending to the saints in the earth (Ps. 16:3); in both the Judge interests himself, rewarding good and punishing hurt to our fellows.

themes: thy wickedness hurts a man like thee
the reckoning between man and man

schools.summary: Henry names Job's complaint (cf. ch. 24:12) and Elihu's solution: the cry fails not through God's deafness but because they ask amiss (James 4:3) — a wailing, not a praying, cry (Hos. 7:14).

Ellicott: among men there is oppression, but not with an almighty Judge, so the course is to wait; Keil and Delitzsch note the address turns on Job, who complained his own prayer went unanswered (ch. 30:20).
Gill: the poor oppressed by the rich, the weak by the mighty, made to cry like Israel under the taskmasters.
Clarke: the wicked rich oppress the wicked poor, who shout for relief yet find none, because they call not on God.

themes: crying against the oppressor, not to God

schools.summary: Gill reads 'my makers' of Father, Son, and Spirit, and laments that scarcely one of the oppressed inquires after God as author, preserver, and benefactor — hence they are not heard.

Clarke gathers the renderings of 'songs in the night' (Chaldee, LXX, Syriac/Arabic, Coverdale) and finds a holy soul's continual communion with God; Wesley: they cry to men but seek not God, who alone can turn darkness to light and give a new song.

Ellicott unsettles the reading: 'songs in the night' may be the reveling oppressor's, not God's, and 'Where is God my Maker?' may be Elihu's own words rather than the oppressed's cry — which he thinks the more intelligible.
Henry presses the devotional point: affliction should quicken us to seek God early (Eccl. 12:1), yet few ever say 'Where is God my Maker?' — all ask where is mirth or wealth.

debates.question: How are 'who giveth songs in the night' and 'Where is God my maker?' to be construed?

sides.position: 'Songs in the night' is God's gift to the afflicted, and 'Where is God my maker?' the cry the oppressed fail to utter
'He who giveth songs in the night' is the reveling oppressor, and 'Where is God my maker?' are Elihu's own words

themes: whose the song and whose the question

schools.summary: Clarke sharpens the rebuke with Isa. 1:3 — the ox knows its owner, but man considers not; beasts have more gratitude than man to his God; Wesley: God gave man wisdom denied the beasts, so leaves him inexcusable for not calling on him.

Henry: reason's chief excellency is that it makes us capable of religion; beasts have instincts but cannot ask 'Where is God my Maker?' — the oppressed who only cry under the arm of the mighty do no more than the brutes (cf. Ps. 104:21).
Gill: the beasts know much, but not so much as man, whom God has raised far above them.
Ellicott offers an alternative rendering, 'who teacheth us by the beasts... and maketh us wise by the fowls,' the creatures our instructors — the oppression the more culpable for forgetting it.

outliers.note: Reads the clause 'who teacheth us BY the beasts of the earth' — the creatures as our instructors — rather than the usual 'more than the beasts.'

themes: crying no better than a brute

schools.summary: Gill: they cry as brutes, without a due sense of God's hand or of his being their only helper, so the cry falls to the ground.

Clarke reads 'from the pride of wicked men' of the oppressors cried against, the prayer failing separately because misdirected; Wesley: God answers not because they are both evil and proud, unhumbled for the sins that brought the misery.
Henry: the criers' own pride stops the cry — God hears not those who regard iniquity (Ps. 66:18) but only the desire of the humble (Ps. 10:17).

debates.question: Whose is 'the pride of evil men' — the oppressors' or the oppressed's?

sides.position: The oppressors' pride, which the afflicted cry against; the prayer fails separately, because misdirected
The criers' own unhumbled pride, which is why God gives no answer

themes: there they cry, but none answers

schools.summary: Gill ranges the senses of 'vanity' — a lie, a rash passionate cry, or vain prayers wrong in matter and manner, not in Christ's name or with sincerity (James 4:3) — which God, requiring truth within, will not hear.
Clarke: God will not attend such vain cries; they cry from their oppressions but not to God, and a cry that never reaches him he cannot be said to hear.
Ellicott: some take the words not as Elihu's verdict but as the oppressed's own despairing cry — 'seeing it is all in vain, God doth not hear.'

outliers.note: Notes the sentence may be read as a continuation of the oppressed's cry from v.12 ('it is all in vain, God doth not hear'), not as Elihu's own principle.

themes: Elihu's verdict or the oppressed's complaint

schools.summary: Gill: the 'not seeing' is not God's essence, nor Christ by faith, nor the beatific vision, but Job's despair of ever seeing God on a throne of judgment to acquit him.

Henry reads two improper senses (not understanding God's dealings, ch. 23:8-9; despairing of his returns, like Hezekiah, Isa. 38:11) and answers with 'judgment is before him' — a coming day when the dark chapters are expounded; therefore trust (Isa. 30:18).

Clarke notes the variants ('see me/us') but keeps the sense: God forgets neither to punish nor to save — be a monument of mercy; Wesley: though God delay, he will do right; repent, humble thyself, and wait.
Ellicott sharpens the first clause to 'thou dost not behold him,' a present blindness the counsel to trust would cure.

themes: unbelief cured by trust not sight

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch keep the received sense — God has visited in anger, and Job in his extremity knows it not; Ellicott owns the clause 'very obscure' and leans the other way — what God's anger visited is nothing to Job's deserts; God has dealt too leniently (judgment not long deferred, ch. 38:1).
Gill keeps 'because it is not so' of Job's want of trust and quiet expectation that God would bring his cause to light and let him behold his righteousness.

Henry: because Job did not trust, the affliction once from love now has displeasure mixed with it; where there is divine wrath in our troubles we may thank our own quarrelling and distrust (Prov. 19:3).
Clarke renders 'because he visiteth not in his anger' — because vengeance is not speedily executed, men are emboldened to iniquity, the very charge Elihu brings against Job.

debates.question: Does the obscure verse say God HAS visited Job in anger, or has NOT (dealing too leniently)?

sides.position: God has visited in anger, because Job would not trust him
God has not visited in anger; his forbearance / unpunished sin has emboldened Job's murmuring

schools.summary: Gill: Job's loud complaints and self-defence were to no purpose, wanting the trust and humility that alone could profit.

Henry: Job opened his mouth in vain, complaining and self-justifying without trust (James 1:7); yet Elihu, unlike the friends, charges him not with hypocrisy but only with Moses's fault of speaking unadvisedly — a mercy to be told, met by recanting not repeating.
Clarke on the delay of vengeance; but candidly owns 'multiplieth words without knowledge' applies not only to Job but to the friends and to Elihu himself — a strife of words.
Keil and Delitzsch render the verse plainly as the closing charge — words heaped without knowledge.

outliers.note: Turns the reproof on the reprovers: 'he multiplieth words without knowledge' applies strongly and generally not only to Job but to the three friends and to Elihu himself — the whole contest a strife of words.

themes: Job openeth his mouth in vain
not hypocrisy but a hasty word
the reproof turned on the reprovers
